title: 50. Sheep behavior and physiology while grazing solar fields: a preliminary assessment.
content:
Abstract
Sheep are increasingly incorporated into solar fields for vegetation management as part of integrated land management strategies. As adoption of solar grazing expands, it is essential to understand how these environments influence livestock performance to ensure animal welfare and productivity. Therefore, the objective of this study was to begin characterizing sheep behavior and physiology while grazing solar fields. A flock of 26 multiparous ewes were weaned onto a solar field and left to graze for ten consecutive days. Water troughs were placed near spigots either in direct sunlight or shaded beneath a solar panel, and water visitation frequency and trough use were recorded using mounted cameras. Bodyweight was measured before and after the grazing period. Daily visual observations were conducted at the coolest and warmest parts of the day to record sheep location (under or outside solar panels) and resting behavior (lying or standing). Temperature and humidity probes were placed under the solar panels and in unobstructed locations and recorded continuously. Heart rate monitors were fitted around the heart girth of 10 randomly selected ewes for a 24h during the grazing period. Sheep visited the unobstructed water trough in direct sunlight more frequently (P < 0.05) than the shaded trough beneath solar panels. Sheep bodyweight decreased (P < 0.05) over the grazing period. The number of sheep located under or outside of the solar panels did not differ by time of day, and lying behavior was not influenced by time of day or location. Standing behavior was not influenced by time of day; however, sheep stood more frequently (P < 0.05) outside of the solar panels compared to under the solar panels. Ambient temperatures were higher (P < 0.05) in the sun than in the shade at both time points. Humidity was lower (P < 0.05) in the sun compared to the shade during the coolest time of day, with no differences in humidity observed at the warmest time of day. Mean heart rate varied by time of day, with higher (P < 0.05) values observed in the warmest part of the day compared to the coolest time of day. Overall, this preliminary study provides insight into sheep behavioral and physiological responses while grazing solar fields, indicating differential use of water resources and shade-associated standing behavior, while heart rate patterns are consistent with diurnal variation rather than elevated stress.
